title: Notations
body_md:
Throughout the paper, we work over a field $\Bbbk$ of characteristic $0$, unless explicitly stated otherwise.
We do not repeat standard definitions 
$\big($Lie algebras, Leibniz algebras, solvable and nilpotent algebras, etc.$\big)$ 
and refer to the literature, see e.g.\ \cite{k23}.
For a set of vectors $S$ we denote by $\big\langle S\big\rangle$ the $\Bbbk$-linear span of $S$.
For the commutator, associator, anti-commutator, and anti-associator, we use
\[
[x,y]=xy-yx,
\qquad
(x,y,z)=(xy)z-x(yz),
\qquad
x\circ y=xy+yx,
\qquad
\{x,y,z\}=(xy)z+x(yz).
\]
When some identities are verified by symbolic computations, we use the computer algebra package {\rm Albert}.
We always assume that algebras under consideration are nontrivial 
$\big($the multiplication is not identically zero$\big)$.
head: manual

title: Definition
body_md:
For a fixed multilinear polynomial 
\begin{center}
    $
\mathfrak f :=\sum\limits_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \alpha_\sigma^j \big(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)}\big)x_{\sigma(3)}+
    \sum\limits_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \beta_\sigma^j x_{\sigma(1)}\big(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)}\big),$
\end{center}   
    we define  that the $\mathfrak M$arseille anti-polynomial 
  $\mathfrak{Ma(f)}$ as follows 
\begin{center}  $
\mathfrak{Ma(f)} :=\sum\limits_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \alpha_\sigma^j \big(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)}\big)x_{\sigma(3)} - 
    \sum\limits_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \beta_\sigma^j x_{\sigma(1)}\big(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)}\big).$ 
\end{center}
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
If a variety of algebras $\rm{Var}$ is defined by the  family $\Omega = \{ f_i\}_{ 1\leq i \leq n}$ of $n$ polynomial identities of degree $3$, then the variety of $\mathfrak M$arseille anti-$\Omega$-algebras $\mathfrak{Ma}$-$\rm{Var}$ is defined by the following family of identities 
    $\mathfrak{Ma}(\Omega)= 
    \big\{ \mathfrak{Ma}(f_i)\big\}_{ 1\leq i \leq n}.$

title: Proposition
body_md: Each $\mathfrak{Ma}$-associative algebra is nilpotent of index $4$.
head: environment

label: basisAAs
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us remember that $\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}\<X\>$ is a $3$-step nilpotent algebra, 
hence, $x_{k_1}\ldots x_{k_t}=0$ for $t \ge 4.$
All basis elements are constructed from words of length $1$, $2$, or $3.$
Due to anti-associativity, all words given by 
$\big\{\ x_{i} (x_{j}x_{k}) \  \big\}_{i,   j, k \in I} $ are independent.
Hence, ${\mathfrak B}$ is a basis of  
$\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}\<X\>.$

title: Proposition
body_md: Each $\mathfrak{Ma}$-shift associative algebra is nilpotent of index $5.$
head: environment

label: basisAAs
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us remember that $\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}S\mathrm{As}\<X\>$ is a $4$-step nilpotent algebra, 
hence, $x_{k_1}\ldots x_{k_t}=0$ for $t \ge 5.$
All basis elements are constructed from words of length $1$, $2$,  $3,$ or $4.$
Due to anti-shift associativity, all words given by 
$\big\{\ x_{i} (x_{j}x_{k}) \  \big\}_{i,   j, k \in I} $ are independent. It is easy to see that 
\begin{longtable}{lclclcl}
$(xy)(zt)$&$=$&$-\  y\big((zt)x\big) $&$=$&$ y \big(t(xz)\big);$ \\ 
$(xy)(zt)$&$=$&$-\ \big(t(xy)\big)z$&$= $&$\big((yt)x\big)z$&$=$&$- \ (xz)(yt).$
\end{longtable}
Hence, ${\mathfrak B}$ is a basis of   $\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}S\mathrm{As}\<X\>.$

head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
For the varieties of $\mathfrak{Ma}$-alternative and $\mathfrak{Ma}$-associative algebras, one has
\[
\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{Alt} \neq \mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}_2 .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is immediate that
\[
\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{Alt} \supseteq \mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}_2 .
\]
To show that the inclusion is strict, we compare the free two-generated algebras
$\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{Alt}\langle a,b\rangle$ and $\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}\langle a,b\rangle$.
Using the computer algebra system Albert, we compute bases of these algebras.

For $\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{Alt}\langle a,b\rangle$ we obtain the following basis elements:
\[
a,\ b,\ bb,\ ba,\ ab,\ aa,
\]
\[
(bb)b,\ (bb)a,\ (ba)b,\ (ab)b,\ (ba)a,\ (ab)a,\ (aa)b,\ (aa)a,
\]
\[
\big((ba)b\big)b,\ \big((ab)a\big)b,\ \big((aa)b\big)b,\ \big((aa)a\big)b.
\]
Moreover, starting from degree $5$ the algebra $\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{Alt}\langle a,b\rangle$ is nilpotent.
On the other hand, by Proposition~\ref{basisAAs}, the algebra
$\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}\langle a,b\rangle$ is nilpotent of index $4$.

Therefore,
\begin{center}
$\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{Alt}\<a,b\>\ncong \mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}_2\<a,b\>$
\ and\ 
$\mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{Alt} \varsupsetneq \mathfrak{Ma}\textrm{-}\mathrm{As}_2.$
\end{center}

label: ExAleib
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ExAleib}
Let us list the set $\mathcal{AL}$ in the multilinear case up to degree $8$. 
Denote by $\mathcal{AL}_i$ the subset of $\mathcal{AL}$ consisting of monomials of degree $i$. 
In degree $3$, we have
\[
\mathcal{AL}_3\ =\ \big\{\,x_{1}(x_{2}x_{3}),\ x_{2}(x_{1}x_{3}),\ x_{3}(x_{1}x_{2}),\ (x_{1}x_{2})x_{3},\ (x_{2}x_{1})x_{3},\ (x_{3}x_{1})x_{2}\,\big\}.
\]
For higher degrees, we indicate only the bracketing type and the number of monomials satisfying the required conditions. If $i=4$, then
\begin{longtable}{lcccr}
$\big((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3}\big)x_{i_4}$&$\rightarrow$&$ {\rm C}_{4}^{1}$&$=$&$4,$\\
$(x_{i_1}x_{i_2})(x_{i_3}x_{i_4})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{4}^{2}\cdot 2$&$=$&$12.$
\end{longtable}
If $i=5$, then
\begin{longtable}{lcccr}
$\big(((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})x_{i_4}\big)x_{i_5}$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{5}^{1}$&$=$&$5,$\\
$\big((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3}\big)(x_{i_4}x_{i_5})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{5}^{3}\cdot 3$&$=$&$30,$\\ 
$\big(x_{i_1}(x_{i_2}x_{i_3})\big)(x_{i_4}x_{i_5})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{5}^{3}\cdot \frac  32$&$=$&$15.$
\end{longtable}
If $i=6$, then
\begin{longtable}{lcccr}
$\big((((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})x_{i_4})x_{i_5}\big)x_{i_6}$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{6}^{1}$&$=$&$6,$\\
$\Big(\big((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3}\big)x_{i_4}\Big)(x_{i_5}x_{i_6})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{6}^{2}\cdot 4$&$=$&$60,$\\ 
$\big((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})(x_{i_3}x_{i_4})\big)(x_{i_5}x_{i_6})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{6}^{4}{\rm C}_{4}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{2}$&$=$&$90.$
\end{longtable}
If $i=7$, then
\begin{longtable}{lcccr}
$\Big(\big((((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})x_{i_4})x_{i_5}\big)x_{i_6}\Big)x_{i_7}$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{7}^{1}$&$=$&$7,$\\
$\Big(\big(((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})x_{i_4}\big)x_{i_5}\Big)(x_{i_6}x_{i_7})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{7}^{2}\cdot 5$&$=$&$105,$\\
$\Big(\big((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3}\big)(x_{i_4}x_{i_5})\Big)(x_{i_6}x_{i_7})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{7}^{2}{\rm C}_{5}^{2}\cdot \frac 32$&$=$&$315,$\\
$\Big(\big(x_{i_1}(x_{i_2}x_{i_3})\big)(x_{i_4}x_{i_5})\Big)(x_{i_6}x_{i_7})$&$\rightarrow$&${\rm C}_{7}^{2}{\rm C}_{5}^{2}{\rm C}_{3}^{2} \cdot \frac 1{3!}$&$=$&$105.$
\end{longtable}
If $i=8$, then
\begin{longtable}{lcccr}
$\Big(\big(((((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})x_{i_4})x_{i_5})x_{i_6}\big)x_{i_7}\Big)x_{i_8} $&$\rightarrow $&${\rm C}^1_8$&$=$&$8,$\\
$\Big(\big((((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})x_{i_4})x_{i_5}\big)x_{i_6}\Big)(x_{i_7}x_{i_8}) $&$\rightarrow $&${\rm C}_{8}^{2} \cdot 6 $&$= $&$168,$\\
$\Big(\big(((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})x_{i_4}\big)(x_{i_5}x_{i_6})\Big)(x_{i_7}x_{i_8}) $&$\rightarrow $&${\rm C}_{8}^{2}{\rm C}_{6}^{2}\cdot \frac 4 2 $&$= $&$840,$\\
$\Big(\big((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})(x_{i_3}x_{i_4})\big)(x_{i_5}x_{i_6})\Big)(x_{i_7}x_{i_8}) $&$\rightarrow $&${\rm C}_{8}^{2}{\rm C}_{6}^{2}{\rm C}_{4}^{2}\cdot \frac 2{3!} $&$= $&$840.$
\end{longtable}
Similarly, we constructed $\mathcal{AL}_9$ and $\mathcal{AL}_{10}$, and obtained
\[
|\mathcal{AL}_9|=6876
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|\mathcal{AL}_{10}|=26200.
\]

label: BasisALeib
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{BasisALeib}
The set $\mathcal{AL}$ is a basis of the algebra $\mathfrak{Ma}$-${\rm Leib\<X\>}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Firstly, we show that the set $\mathcal{AL}$ spans $\mathfrak{Ma}$-${\rm Leib}\<X\>$. 
Let $m$ be an arbitrary monomial of degree $k$ of the form
\[
m\ =\ \big(\cdots((x_i w_1)w_2)\cdots\big)w_n.
\]
Using the identities \eqref{ALeib2} and \eqref{ALeib3}, we can reduce $m$ whenever $\deg(w_j)\ge 3$. Using the identity \eqref{ALeib1}, we order the generators inside $w_j$. 
Next, we can interchange $w_j$ and $w_{j+1}$ by the defining identity of $\mathfrak{Ma}$-${\rm Leib}\<X\>$, namely,
\[
(aw_j)w_{j+1}=a(w_{j+1}w_{j})+(aw_{j+1})w_{j}.
\]
If both $w_j$ and $w_{j+1}$ are generators and $w_j>w_{j+1}$, then the monomials
$a(w_{j+1}w_{j})$ and $(aw_{j+1})w_{j}$ belong to $\mathcal{AL}$. 
If $\deg(w_{j})=\deg(w_{j+1})=2$, then the identity above reduces to
\[
(aw_j)w_{j+1}=(aw_{j+1})w_{j}.
\]
Thus, the set of remaining monomials coincides with the set $\mathcal{AL}$.

Let us consider the algebra $\mathcal{A}\<X\>$ with a basis $\mathcal{AL}$. 
We define a multiplication on $\mathcal{A}\<X\>$ as follows. 
Let $A_i\in\mathcal{AL}$ be an arbitrary basis monomial of degree $i$.

\begin{itemize}
\item If $A_t\in\mathcal{AL}$ has degree $t\ge 3$, then
\[
A_k\cdot A_t=0
\qquad (k\ge 1).
\]

\item If $t=2$, and
\[
A_k\ =\ \big(\cdots((x_i w_1)w_2)\cdots\big)w_n,
\]
then for any degree-$2$ basis monomial $w_p$ we set
\[
A_k\cdot w_p
=\big(\cdots((((\cdots((x_i w_1)w_2)\cdots)w_{r-1})w_p)w_r)\cdots\big)w_n,
\]
where $w_{r-1}\le w_p\le w_r$.

\item If $t=1$, and
\[
A_k=\big(\cdots(((\cdots((x_i x_{t_1})x_{t_2})\cdots)x_{t_l})w_{l+1})\cdots\big)w_n,
\]
then for any generator $x_p$ we define
\begin{multline*}
A_k\cdot x_p
=\big(\cdots(((\cdots((((\cdots((x_i x_{t_1})x_{t_2})\cdots)x_{t_{r-1}})x_p)x_{t_r})\cdots)x_{t_l})w_{l+1})\cdots\big)w_n \\
+\sum_{s=r}^{l}\big(\cdots((((\cdots(((\cdots((x_i x_{t_1})x_{t_2})\cdots)x_{t_{r-1}})x_{t_r})\cdots)x_{t_l})(x_p x_{t_s}))w_{l+1})\cdots\big)w_n,
\end{multline*}
where $x_{t_{r-1}}\le x_p<x_{t_r}$, and in the final sum there is no generator $x_{t_s}$ among $x_{t_r},\dots,x_{t_l}$.
\end{itemize}
A direct computation shows that the algebra $\mathcal{A}\<X\>$ belongs to $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Leib}$, that is, it satisfies the defining identity of $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Leib}$. 
It remains to note that
\[
\mathcal{A}\<X\>\cong \mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}{\rm Leib}\<X\>.
\]

title: Proposition
body_md: Each $\big($left$\big)$ $\mathfrak{Ma}$-Zinbiel algebra is a $\big($left$\big)$ conservative algebra  with the  additional multiplication given by $a*b\ =\ -\ (ab+ba).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Thanks to Proposition \ref{arz},
each left $\mathfrak{Ma}$-Zinbiel algebra is left-commutative.
Thanks to \cite{KLP15}, each left-conservative algebra
that satisfies a quasi-identity 
\begin{center}
    $a(bx)\  =\  {\rm F}(a, b)x$
\end{center} for a new multiplication $F$ is a conservative. 
Hence, our left $\mathfrak{Ma}$-Zinbiel algebra is conservative with the additional multiplication  ${\rm F}(a,b)\ =\ -\ (ab+ba).$

label: ANovGenId
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ANovGenId}
For any $n\ge 5$, the following identity holds in $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Nov}\<X\>$:
\[
x_{i_1}\bigl(((\cdots((x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{3}})x_{i_{4}})\cdots)x_{i_{n-1}})x_{i_n}\bigr)
=
x_{i_2}\bigl(((\cdots((x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{n-1}})x_{i_{n-2}})\cdots)x_{i_{3}})x_{i_n}\bigr).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using the left-commutative identity and \eqref{ANovId1}, we obtain
\begin{multline*}
x_{i_1}\bigl(((\cdots((x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{3}})x_{i_{4}})\cdots)x_{i_{n-1}})x_{i_n}\bigr)
=
\big((\cdots((x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{3}})x_{i_{4}})\cdots)x_{i_{n-1}}\big)(x_{i_1}x_{i_n})
\\
=
\big((\cdots((x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{3}})x_{i_{4}})\cdots)x_{i_{n-2}}\big)\bigl((x_{i_1}x_{i_{n-1}})x_{i_n}\bigr).
\end{multline*}
Now we apply \eqref{ANovId1} repeatedly:
\begin{multline*}
\big((\cdots((x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{3}})x_{i_{4}})\cdots)x_{i_{n-2}}\big)\bigl((x_{i_1}x_{i_{n-1}})x_{i_n}\bigr)
\\
=
\big((\cdots((x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{3}})x_{i_{4}})\cdots)x_{i_{n-3}}\big)\bigl(((x_{i_1}x_{i_{n-1}})x_{i_{n-2}})x_{i_n}\bigr)
=\ldots
\\
=
x_{i_2}\bigl(((\cdots((x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{n-1}})x_{i_{n-2}})\cdots)x_{i_{3}})x_{i_n}\bigr).
\end{multline*}
head: environment

label: ThmANovBasis
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{ThmANovBasis}
The basis of $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Nov}\<X\>$ coincides with the basis of the free bicommutative algebra ${\rm BiCom}\<X\>$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we show that every monomial in $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Nov}\<X\>$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of monomials from $\mathcal{AN}$.
We prove this by induction on the degree.

The base cases are $n=3$ and $n=4$. For $n=3$, we have
\[
x_{2}(x_{1}x_{3})=x_{1}(x_{2}x_{3}),\qquad
x_{3}(x_{2}x_{1})=x_{2}(x_{3}x_{1}),\qquad
x_{3}(x_{1}x_{2})=x_{1}(x_{3}x_{2}),
\]
and
\[
(x_{1}x_{2})x_{3}=(x_{1}x_{3})x_{2}+x_{1}(x_{3}x_{2})-x_{1}(x_{2}x_{3}),
\]
\[
(x_{2}x_{1})x_{3}=(x_{2}x_{3})x_{1}+x_{2}(x_{3}x_{1})-x_{1}(x_{2}x_{3}),
\]
\[
(x_{3}x_{1})x_{2}=(x_{3}x_{2})x_{1}+x_{2}(x_{3}x_{1})-x_{1}(x_{3}x_{2}).
\]

We endow $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Nov}\<X\>$ with the degree--lexicographical order.
We also write $m\equiv m'$ if $m$ and $m'$ have the same bracketing type and
$m-m'$ is a linear combination of basis monomials strictly smaller than $m$ in this order.
In degree $3$, this yields
\[
(x_{1}x_{2})x_{3}\equiv (x_{1}x_{3})x_{2},\qquad
(x_{2}x_{1})x_{3}\equiv (x_{2}x_{3})x_{1},\qquad
(x_{3}x_{1})x_{2}\equiv (x_{3}x_{2})x_{1}.
\]
As example, the identity \eqref{ANovId3} shows that
\[
(db)\big((ce)a\big)\equiv 0.
\]

For $n=4$, by the left-commutative identity, every monomial of the form
$x_{i_1}\bigl(x_{i_2}(x_{i_3}x_{i_4})\bigr)$ can be rewritten as one of the following monomials:
\[
x_{1}\bigl(x_{2}(x_{3}x_{4})\bigr),\quad
x_{1}\bigl(x_{2}(x_{4}x_{3})\bigr),\quad
x_{1}\bigl(x_{3}(x_{4}x_{2})\bigr),\quad
x_{2}\bigl(x_{3}(x_{4}x_{1})\bigr).
\]

For a monomial of the form $x_{i_1}\bigl((x_{i_2}x_{i_3})x_{i_4}\bigr)$, using the inductive hypothesis and \eqref{ANovId1}, we obtain
\[
x_{i_1}\bigl((x_{i_2}x_{i_3})x_{i_4}\bigr)\equiv
x_{i_1}\bigl((x_{i_2}x_{i_4})x_{i_3}\bigr)
=
x_{i_2}\bigl((x_{i_1}x_{i_4})x_{i_3}\bigr).
\]
In particular, modulo $\equiv$, we can permute the generators within the pairs $(x_{i_1},x_{i_2})$ and $(x_{i_3},x_{i_4})$ in order to achieve the required ordering.

Next, consider a monomial of the form $(x_{i_1}x_{i_2})(x_{i_3}x_{i_4})$.
By the left-commutative identity and the inductive hypothesis, we have
\[
(x_{i_1}x_{i_2})(x_{i_3}x_{i_4})\equiv 0,
\]
that is, there is no basis monomial with the same bracketing type, and this monomial can be expressed as a linear combination of smaller basis monomials.

Similarly, by \eqref{ANovId2} and the previous cases, we have
\[
\bigl(x_{i_1}(x_{i_2}x_{i_3})\bigr)x_{i_4}\equiv 0.
\]

Finally, using the defining identities of $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Nov}$ together with the previous reductions, we obtain
\[
\bigl((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3}\bigr)x_{i_4}
\equiv
\bigl((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_4}\bigr)x_{i_3}
\equiv
\bigl((x_{i_1}x_{i_4})x_{i_2}\bigr)x_{i_3}.
\]
This completes the verification of the base case $n=4$.

Let $n\ge 5$. We consider products $A_pA_{n-p}$, where $A_k$ denotes an arbitrary monomial of degree $k$.

\smallskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 1: $A_1A_{n-1}$.}
By the inductive hypothesis, every monomial of the form $A_1A_{n-1}$ can be written as
\[
x_{i_1}\Bigl(x_{i_2}\bigl(\cdots\bigl(x_{i_k}((\cdots((x_{i_{k+1}}x_{i_{k+2}})x_{i_{k+3}})\cdots)x_{i_n})\bigr)\cdots\bigr)\Bigr).
\]
Applying Lemma \ref{ANovGenId}, we obtain
\begin{multline*}
x_{i_1}\Bigl(x_{i_2}\bigl(\cdots\bigl(x_{i_k}((\cdots((x_{i_{k+1}}x_{i_{k+2}})x_{i_{k+3}})\cdots)x_{i_n})\bigr)\cdots\bigr)\Bigr)
\equiv\\
x_{i_1}\Bigl(x_{i_2}\bigl(\cdots\bigl(x_{i_{k+1}}((\cdots((x_{i_k}x_{i_{k+2}})x_{i_{k+3}})\cdots)x_{i_n})\bigr)\cdots\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{multline*}
Hence, using the left-commutative identity and Lemma \ref{ANovGenId}, we can reorder (modulo $\equiv$) the generators
\[
x_{i_1},x_{i_2},\ldots,x_{i_{k+1}}
\]
to achieve the required nondecreasing order.
Moreover, by the inductive hypothesis, the generators
\[
x_{i_{k+2}},x_{i_{k+3}},\ldots,x_{i_n}
\]
can also be ordered (modulo $\equiv$) in the t

\smallskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 2: $A_tA_{n-t}$ with $t>1$ and $n-t>1$.}
By \eqref{ANovId1}, we have
\[
A_tA_{n-t}\equiv 0,
\]
that is, such monomials reduce to a linear combination of smaller basis monomials.

\smallskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 3: $A_{n-1}A_1$.}
By \eqref{ANovId2}, every monomial in $A_{n-1}A_1$ vanishes modulo $\equiv$, except the fully left-normed monomial
\[
\big(\cdots((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})\cdots\big)x_{i_n}.
\]
For a monomial of this form, by the previous reductions, we can permute the indices $i_2,\ldots,i_n$ modulo $\equiv$; more precisely,
\[
\big(\cdots((x_{i_1}x_{i_2})x_{i_3})\cdots\big)x_{i_n}\equiv
\big(\cdots((x_{i_1}x_{i_{\sigma(2)}})x_{i_{\sigma(3)}})\cdots\big)x_{i_{\sigma(n)}},
\qquad \sigma\in \mathbb{S}_{\{2,3,\ldots,n\}}.
\]
This completes the inductive step.

Let us consider the algebra $\mathcal{A}\langle X\rangle$ with basis $\mathcal{AN}$.
We define a bilinear multiplication on $\mathcal{A}\langle X\rangle$ on basis elements as follows.

Let $x_{i_{k+2}},\ldots,x_{i_{n}},y_{j_{l+2}},\ldots,y_{j_{m-1}}\geq y_{j_m}$,
\[
u=
x_{i_1}\bigl(x_{i_2}(\cdots(x_{i_k}L_x)\cdots)\bigr),
\qquad
L_x=\big(\cdots((x_{i_{k+1}}x_{i_{k+2}})x_{i_{k+3}})\cdots\big)x_{i_n},
\]
and
\[
v=
y_{j_1}\bigl(y_{j_2}(\cdots(y_{j_l}L_y)\cdots)\bigr),
\qquad
L_y=\big(\cdots((y_{j_{l+1}}y_{j_{l+2}})y_{j_{l+3}})\cdots)y_{j_m}.
\]
Set
\[
uv=
z_{p_1}\bigl(z_{p_2}(\cdots(z_{p_{k+l+1}}L_z)\cdots)\bigr),
\qquad
L_z=((\cdots((z_{p_{k+l+2}}z_{p_{k+l+3}})z_{p_{k+l+4}})\cdots)z_{p_{n+m-1}}\big)y_{j_m},
\]
where the indices are determined by the following conditions:
\[
\{x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_{k+1}},\,y_{j_1},\ldots,y_{j_{l+1}}\}
=
\{z_{p_1},\ldots,z_{p_{k+l+2}}\},
\]
\[
\{x_{i_{k+2}},\ldots,x_{i_n},\,y_{j_{l+2}},\ldots,y_{j_{m-1}}\}
=
\{z_{p_{k+l+3}},\ldots,z_{p_{n+m-1}}\},
\]
and the variables are ordered so that
\[
z_{p_1}\le \cdots \le z_{p_{k+l+2}},
\qquad
z_{p_{k+l+3}}\ge \cdots \ge z_{p_{n+m-1}}.
\]
Equivalently, the first block is written in nondecreasing order, while the second block is written in nonincreasing order.

The only remaining case is when, in the tail $L_z$, the element $y_{j_m}$ occurs inside the nonincreasing block, namely,
\[
z_{p_{k+l+3}}\ge \cdots \ge z_{p_r}\ge y_{j_m} \ge z_{p_{r+1}}\ge \cdots \ge z_{p_{n+m-1}}.
\]
Without loss of generality, we assume that $y_{j_m} \ge z_{p_{k+l+3}}\ge \cdots \ge z_{p_{n+m-1}}.$
As a result, $L_z$ can be written as the following alternating sum:
\begin{multline*}
L_z=\big((\cdots((z_{p_{k+l+2}}z_{p_{k+l+3}})z_{p_{k+l+4}})\cdots)z_{p_{n+m-1}}\big)y_{j_m}\\
=\big(\cdots(((z_{p_{k+l+2}}y_{j_m})z_{p_{k+l+3}})z_{p_{k+l+4}})\cdots\big)z_{p_{n+m-1}}\\
\quad +\,z_{p_{k+l+2}}\bigl((\cdots((y_{j_m}z_{p_{k+l+3}})z_{p_{k+l+4}})\cdots)z_{p_{n+m-1}}\bigr)
-\,z_{p_{k+l+2}}\bigl((\cdots((z_{p_{n+m-1}}y_{j_m})z_{p_{k+l+3}})\cdots)z_{p_{n+m-2}}\bigr)\\
\quad -\,z_{p_{k+l+2}}\Bigl(z_{p_{n+m-1}}\bigl((\cdots((y_{j_m}z_{p_{k+l+3}})z_{p_{k+l+4}})\cdots)z_{p_{n+m-2}}\bigr)\Bigr)\\
\quad +\,z_{p_{k+l+2}}\Bigl(z_{p_{n+m-1}}\bigl((\cdots((z_{p_{n+m-2}}y_{j_m})z_{p_{k+l+3}})\cdots)z_{p_{n+m-3}}\bigr)\Bigr)
\;+\;\cdots\\
\quad +\,(-1)^n z_{p_{k+l+2}}\Bigl(z_{p_{n+m-1}}\bigl(z_{p_{n+m-2}}(\cdots(y_{j_m}z_{p_{k+l+3}})\cdots)\bigr)\Bigr)\\
\quad -\,(-1)^n z_{p_{k+l+2}}\Bigl(z_{p_{n+m-1}}\bigl(z_{p_{n+m-2}}(\cdots(z_{p_{k+l+3}}y_{j_m})\cdots)\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{multline*}

We illustrate this expansion with several low-degree examples:
\[
\big((ac)b\big)d=
\big((ad)c\big)b+a\bigl((dc)b\bigr)-a\bigl((bd)c\bigr)-a\bigl(b(dc)\bigr)+a\bigl(b(cd)\bigr),
\]
\begin{multline*}
\big(((ad)c)b\big)e
=\big(((ae)d)c\big)b+a\bigl(((ed)c)b\bigr)-a\bigl(((be)d)c\bigr)-a\bigl(b((ed)c)\bigr)+a\bigl(b((ce)d)\bigr)\\
\qquad\qquad
+a\bigl(b(c(ed))\bigr)-a\bigl(b(c(de))\bigr),
\end{multline*}
and
\begin{multline*}
((((ae)d)c)b)f
=((((af)e)d)c)b+a\bigl((((fe)d)c)b\bigr)-a\bigl((((bf)e)d)c\bigr)-a\bigl(b(((fe)d)c)\bigr)\\
+a\bigl(b(((cf)e)d)\bigr)
+a\bigl(b(c((fe)d))\bigr)-a\bigl(b(c((df)e))\bigr)
-a\bigl(b(c(d(fe)))\bigr)+a\bigl(b(c(d(ef)))\bigr).
\end{multline*}


A direct computation shows that the algebra $\mathcal{A}\<X\>$ belongs to $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Nov}$, that is, it satisfies the defining identity of $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$${\rm Nov}$. 
It remains to note that

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\mathrm{Var}$ be a quadratic operad over a field $\Bbbk$ with
$\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2$. Then
\[
(\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var})^{(!)}\ =\ 
\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}(\mathrm{Var}^{(!)}).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathrm{Var}=\mathcal F(E)/(R)$ be a quadratic presentation, where $\mathcal F(E)$ is the free symmetric operad
generated by a binary $\mathbb S$-module $E$ and $R\subset \mathcal F(E)(3)$ is the $\mathbb S_3$-submodule of
quadratic relations. We use the definition of the quadratic dual operad via orthogonal complement:
\[
\mathrm{Var}^{(!)}=\mathcal F(E^{\vee})/(R^{\perp}),
\qquad
R^{\perp}:=\{\,g\in \mathcal F(E^{\vee})(3)\mid \langle r,g\rangle=0\ \text{for all } r\in R\,\},
\]
where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the standard nondegenerate $\mathbb S_3$-invariant pairing
between $\mathcal F(E)(3)$ and $\mathcal F(E^{\vee})(3)$.

In arity $3$, we have the direct sum decomposition
\[
\mathcal F(E)(3)=\mathcal F_L(E)(3)\oplus \mathcal F_R(E)(3),
\]
where $\mathcal F_L(E)(3)$ is spanned by the monomials
$\bigl(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)}\bigr)x_{\sigma(3)}$ and
$\mathcal F_R(E)(3)$ is spanned by the monomials
$x_{\sigma(1)}\bigl(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)}\bigr)$, for $\sigma\in\mathbb S_3$.
Hence every $f\in \mathcal F(E)(3)$ is uniquely written as $f=f_L+f_R$ with
$f_L\in \mathcal F_L(E)(3)$ and $f_R\in \mathcal F_R(E)(3)$.

By definition,
\[
\mathfrak{Ma}(f):=f_L-f_R.
\]
In particular, $\mathfrak{Ma}$ is $\Bbbk$-linear, $\mathbb S_3$-equivariant, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:MaProperties}
\mathfrak{Ma}^2=\mathrm{id},\qquad
\mathfrak{Ma}\big|_{\mathcal F_L(E)(3)}=\mathrm{id},\qquad
\mathfrak{Ma}\big|_{\mathcal F_R(E)(3)}=-\,\mathrm{id}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, since $\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2$, we have the projections
\begin{equation*}
f_L=\frac12\bigl(f+\mathfrak{Ma}(f)\bigr),
\qquad
f_R=\frac12\bigl(f-\mathfrak{Ma}(f)\bigr).
\end{equation*}

We define $\mathfrak{Ma}$ on $\mathcal F(E^{\vee})(3)$ by the same rule:
it acts by $+1$ on the left-nested component and by $-1$ on the right-nested component.
Then for all $f\in\mathcal F(E)(3)$ and $g\in\mathcal F(E^{\vee})(3)$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:MaAdjoint}
\langle \mathfrak{Ma}(f),\,g\rangle=\langle f,\,\mathfrak{Ma}(g)\rangle.
\end{equation}
Indeed, writing $f=f_L+f_R$ and $g=g_L+g_R$, we obtain
\[
\langle \mathfrak{Ma}(f),g\rangle
=\langle f_L-f_R,\,g_L+g_R\rangle
=\langle f_L,g_L\rangle-\langle f_R,g_R\rangle,
\]
because the mixed pairings $\langle f_L,g_R\rangle$ and $\langle f_R,g_L\rangle$ vanish.
On the other hand,
\[
\langle f,\mathfrak{Ma}(g)\rangle
=\langle f_L+f_R,\,g_L-g_R\rangle
=\langle f_L,g_L\rangle-\langle f_R,g_R\rangle,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:MaAdjoint}.

We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:OrthCommutesMa}
\bigl(\mathfrak{Ma}(R)\bigr)^{\perp}=\mathfrak{Ma}\bigl(R^{\perp}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Let $g\in \big(\mathfrak{Ma}(R)\big)^{\perp}$. Then for every $r\in R$ we have
\[
\langle \mathfrak{Ma}(r),\,g\rangle=0.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:MaAdjoint}, this is equivalent to $\langle r,\,\mathfrak{Ma}(g)\rangle=0$ for all $r\in R$,
hence $\mathfrak{Ma}(g)\in R^{\perp}$. Applying \eqref{eq:MaProperties}, we get
$g=\mathfrak{Ma}\big(\mathfrak{Ma}(g)\big)\in \mathfrak{Ma}(R^{\perp})$.
Thus $\big(\mathfrak{Ma}(R)\big)^{\perp}\subseteq \mathfrak{Ma}(R^{\perp})$.

Conversely, let $g\in \mathfrak{Ma}(R^{\perp})$. Then $g=\mathfrak{Ma}(h)$ for some $h\in R^{\perp}$.
For any $r\in R$ we obtain, using \eqref{eq:MaAdjoint} and \eqref{eq:MaProperties},
\[
\langle \mathfrak{Ma}(r),\,g\rangle
=\langle \mathfrak{Ma}(r),\,\mathfrak{Ma}(h)\rangle
=\langle r,\,h\rangle
=0.
\]
Hence $g\in \big(\mathfrak{Ma}(R)\big)^{\perp}$, and therefore
$\mathfrak{Ma}(R^{\perp})\subseteq \big(\mathfrak{Ma}(R)\big)^{\perp}$.
This proves \eqref{eq:OrthCommutesMa}.

title: Theorem
body_md: The operad $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var}$ satisfies the Dong property if and only if $\mathrm{Var}$ satisfies the Dong property.
head: environment

label: eq:ToInside
title: Proof
body_md:
We use the criterion from \cite{Dong}. Namely, an operad $\mathrm{Var}$ satisfies the Dong property if and only if $\mathrm{Var}$ fulfills the identities
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ToInside}
(x_1\circ_j x_2)\circ_i x_3
=\sum_{k,l\in I}
\alpha^{i,j}_{k,l}\,(x_3\circ_k x_2)\circ_l x_1
+\beta^{i,j}_{k,l}\,(x_1\circ_k x_3)\circ_l x_2,
\end{equation}
where, for each $t\in\{i,j,k,l\}$, the operation $\circ_t$ is either the operation $\cdot$ of $\mathrm{Var}$ or its opposite operation, that is,
$\circ_t=\cdot$ or $\circ_t=\cdot^{op}$.
Thus, if $\mathrm{Var}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:ToInside}, then the operad $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var}$ satisfies the analogous identity, where each monomial involving
$\circ_i=\cdot^{op}$ and $\circ_l=\cdot^{op}$ appears with the opposite sign.
Nevertheless, the operad $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var}$ still satisfies \eqref{eq:ToInside}.

body_md: Among the algebras listed in the table above, the operads $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$associative, $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$shift-associative, $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$assosymmetric, $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$Novikov, and $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}$alternative are precisely those that satisfy the Dong property.

label: MaVar-left
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The implication $(\Leftarrow)$ follows immediately from the definition.
Indeed, if the defining identities of $\mathrm{Var}$ can be chosen in the form \eqref{MaVar-left} and \eqref{MaVar-right}, then applying $\mathfrak{Ma}$ fixes every identity of the form \eqref{MaVar-left} and changes the sign of every identity of the form \eqref{MaVar-right}. Hence the same family of identities defines both $\mathrm{Var}$ and $\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var}$, and therefore $\mathrm{Var}=\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var}$.

\smallskip
To prove $(\Rightarrow)$, assume that $\mathrm{Var}=\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var}$. Let $f$ be any defining multilinear identity of degree $3$ for $\mathrm{Var}$. Then $f$ has the form
\[
f=\sum_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \alpha_\sigma \bigl(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)}\bigr)x_{\sigma(3)}
+\sum_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \beta_\sigma \,x_{\sigma(1)}\bigl(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)}\bigr)=0.
\]
Since $\mathrm{Var}=\mathfrak{Ma}\text{-}\mathrm{Var}$, the operad $\mathrm{Var}$ also satisfies the identity $\mathfrak{Ma}(f)=0$, that is,
\[
\sum_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \alpha_\sigma \bigl(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)}\bigr)x_{\sigma(3)}
-\sum_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \beta_\sigma \,x_{\sigma(1)}\bigl(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)}\bigr)=0.
\]
Assuming $\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2$ (in particular, in characteristic $0$), adding these two identities we obtain
\[
\sum_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \alpha_\sigma \bigl(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)}\bigr)x_{\sigma(3)}=0,
\]
and subtracting the second identity from the first one we obtain
\[
\sum_{\sigma \in \mathbb{S}_3} \beta_\sigma \,x_{\sigma(1)}\bigl(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)}\bigr)=0.
\]
Thus, the defining identities of $\mathrm{Var}$ can be chosen separately in the left-bracketed form \eqref{MaVar-left} and the right-bracketed form \eqref{MaVar-right}, as required.

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let ${\rm A}$ be an algebra, then 
$\mathfrak{aff}^+({\rm A})$ is Jacobi--Jordan if and only if
${\rm A}$ is $\mathcal{M}a$-Novikov.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak{aff}^+({\rm A})$ be Jacobi--Jordan and  $a_1, a_2, a_3 \in {\rm A},$ then 
    \begin{longtable}{lll}
$(a_1t^{n_1} \circ a_2 t^{n_2}) \circ a_3 t^{n_3}$&$=$&$
n_1(n_1+n_2-1)\ (a_1a_2)a_3+n_1n_3 \ a_3(a_1a_2)+$\\
\multicolumn{3}{r}{$n_2(n_1+n_2-1)\ (a_2a_1)a_3
+n_2n_3 \ a_3(a_2a_1);$}\\

$(a_2t^{n_2} \circ a_3 t^{n_3}) \circ a_1 t^{n_1}$&$=$&$
n_2(n_2+n_3-1)\ (a_2a_3)a_1+n_2n_1 \ a_1(a_2a_3)+$\\
\multicolumn{3}{r}{$n_3(n_2+n_3-1)\ (a_3a_2)a_1
+n_3n_1 \ a_1(a_3a_2);$}\\


$(a_3t^{n_3} \circ a_1 t^{n_1}) \circ a_2 t^{n_2}$&$=$&$
n_3(n_3+n_1-1)\ (a_3a_1)a_2+n_3n_2 \ a_2(a_3a_1)+$\\
\multicolumn{3}{r}{$n_1(n_3+n_1-1)\ (a_1a_3)a_2
+n_1n_2 \ a_2(a_1a_3).$}\\
    \end{longtable}
Summarizing the above relations and using the Jacobi--Jordan identity
\begin{enumerate}
    \item for $n_2=n_3=0,$ we have $(a_1a_2)a_3 = - (a_1a_2)a_3.$

    \item for $n_1=0,$ we have 
  
$n_2(n_2-1) \ (a_2a_1)a_3 + 
n_2n_3 \ a_3(a_2a_1) +
n_2(n_2+n_3-1) \ (a_2a_3)a_1 +
 $
\begin{flushright}
$n_3(n_2+n_3-1) \ (a_3a_2)a_1 + 
n_3(n_3-1) \ (a_3a_1)a_2 +
    n_3n_2 \ a_2(a_3a_1)=0.$
 \end{flushright}
   
The last is equivalent to 
$\big\{a_3,a_2,a_1 \big\} = - \big\{a_2,a_3,a_1\big\}.$\end{enumerate}
Hence, ${\rm A}$ is $\mathcal{M}a$-Novikov.
On the other side, it is easy to see that for each
$\mathcal{M}a$-Novikov, its symmetric affinization gives a Jacobi--Jordan algebra.
